newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: CZECH FINMIN LATEST RESULTS SHOW 96 BUDGET DEFICIT.
newsitem.headline: CZECH FINMIN LATEST RESULTS SHOW 96 BUDGET DEFICIT.

text.p: The Czech 1996 state budget was in deficit by 1.7 billion crowns as of January 14, one day before the deadline for entities to bill the state for services provdided during the year, a Finance Ministry official said on Wednesday.
"(We expect) the definitive results for 1996 will range around a deficit of 1.7 billion crowns," said Miroslav Havel, deputy finance minister, in testimony to the parliamentary budget committtee.
He said that as of January 14, revenues for the state totalled 482.8 billion crowns, while expenditures were 484.5 billion crowns.
Havel added that some additional bills may be delivered in the days following the deadline, which could inflate expenditures further.

Parliamentary budget committee chairman Jozef Wagner said at the session that though he was not upset with the slight deficit in 1996, he was concerned with the effects any changes in payments may have on the 1997 budget.
The deficit does not come as a shock to many since the government said in December that it was trying to hold an expected deficit to around one billion crowns.

But last week, the Czech government delayed payments and forced some early collections, including a 650 million crown early repayment on credit to the Deposit Insurance Fund in an attempt to allow it to claim its fourth straight budget surplus in 1996.

Ministries were also asked to save as much as possible in December, and banks Ceska Sporitelna a.s. and IPB a.s. agreed to delay their receipt of 800 million crowns in state support on housing loans. Both banks are partially privatised, but the State still holds major stakes in each.
Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus, who calls balanced budgets the "alpha and omega" of his government, has praised the figures as a sign of the country's continued fiscal responsibility.
The 1996 budget was originally approved as a balanced budget totalling 497.6 billion crowns, but autumn spending cuts knocked the forecast expenditure down to 491 billion crowns.
Parliament approved a fifth straight balanced budget plan in December, with both expenditures and revenues forecast at 549.1 billion crowns in 1997.

But the 1997 budget was based on economic growth of 5.4 percent, and many independent analysts have forecast growth for this year at under five percent, after growth between 4.0 and 4.5 percent for the whole of 1996.
Many have voiced concern that slower than expected economic growth might force the government to consider major changes in the 1997 budget to keep Klaus's budget record entact.
